utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. Could you call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Yes, I can follow you in the language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Now, I have a long list, I see, on both sides. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we couldn't resist it on a day like today. Joanna Korner, assisted by Ann Sutherland, Julian Nicholls, and Colin Black, Your Honours may recall, to do the journalist case. He had a great deal to do with the writing of the brief. And also, as ever, Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner, and welcome back. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. It's nice to see you all again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Same here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm glad to be back. My name is John Ackerman, in case you've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Speak for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I represent Mr. Brdjanin. I'm here with Aleksandar Vujic, our case manager, and the person sitting next to him is not David Cunningham. Mr. Cunningham left this morning for the United States. I'd like you to meet Ross Pytlik. Ross is a student at Hastings University in -- in San Francisco, California and is here as an intern with our team for a while, for a few months. And so he's come to court with us today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And welcome, Mr. Pytlik. And welcome, Mr. Black. So I think we have a pretty much specific programme to go through today. We will start with the oral decision on the Rule 98 bis motion. And then we'll proceed from that. So this is an oral decision on the confidential motion for judgement of acquittal under Rule -- filed under Rule 98 bis. And which was actually filed on the 22nd of August of 2003, to which the Prosecution filed a confidential Prosecutor's response to defendant Radoslav Brdjanin on the 5th of September and -- and then this was followed by a public Prosecutor's motion in respect of a response to the accused's motion on the 2nd of October. As you may imagine, the written decision, as we had explained before the summer recess, will -- will follow this oral decision. I can't tell you the specific date, but I should be able to tell you exactly when the -- when to expect the written decision. It's being worked upon, and it's already at a pretty advanced stage. And I also need to advise you straight away that only the written decision will be the authoritative document on the Rule 98 bis motion. One other preliminary thing that I think I should make clear is that today's oral decision is being limited to the basic dispositions related to the various counts of the indictment, and specifically arising from the submissions of the accused based in the motion under Rule 98 bis that there should be an acquittal on each count. As you are aware, various points of law were raised, both by the Defence and by the Prosecution in the documents that were filed. These have all been considered -- given due consideration by the Trial Chamber in its -- in our discussions and deliberations. Of course, you don't expect us to say anything much about these -- our decisions on these points of law now in this oral decision, because as I explained, this is more or less -- we are pronouncing ourselves on the -- whether there should be an acquittal on each and every count and not much more, but there are some points, some relating to some issues that were raised that we will need to touch upon as we go on this afternoon. All these point will be addressed fully in the written decision. The first thing -- or the first matter that we need to make clear is that in our deliberations and in our decisions we based ourselves on the standard that has been established more or less and which has been referred to and agreed to by both of you. That's the standard set down in the Jelesic Appeal Chamber decision of the 5th of July, 2001. I don't think I need to read the standard. You are aware of it. And you have basically agreed, both of you, that this should be the standard that the Trial Chamber was expected, according to you, to follow. There are some preliminary matters that we took into consideration and which I am going to hint at, and that's mainly the fact that as it arises from your motion, Mr. Ackerman, the Defence was not contesting the occurrence of certain specific incidents alleged by the Prosecution in the indictment, not challenging, not contesting that they may have taken -- or that they have taken place. In addition to this, however, we have carried out a complete exercise ourselves over and above your declaration, and one of the basic conclusions that we come to at this stage and for the purpose of Rule 98 bis standards only is that we find that a reasonable trier of fact could find the Prosecution evidence on these facts as sufficient to -- to sustain a conviction beyond reasonable doubt if, of course, the other ingredients of the offences are satisfied. One of the focal points that conditioned more or less the whole exercise, the entire exercise that we embarked upon was Appendix C which was appended to the Prosecution's response. And in it the Prosecution conceded that sufficient evidence had not been produced with regard to a number of criminal acts charged in the indictment. This appendix was divided into two parts. The first part, which is referred to as part A, relates to criminal acts -- all criminal acts in the municipalities of Bihac-Ripac, Bosanska Dubica, and Bosanska Gradiska. The second part, which I will be referring to as appendix -- as part B of Appendix C, related to the destruction and willful damage of Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat religious and cultural buildings, as charged in paragraphs 47(3)(b), 62 and 63 of the indictment. As you can certainly imagine -- as certainly you are aware, the legal consequences of Appendix C of these concessions, which the Prosecution made, the legal consequence is that some counts of the indictment are necessarily -- are necessarily affected, and we are going to start precisely with this. For the purpose of brevity, the concessions will be dealt with together, rather than addressing parts A and B separately. So we're putting everything in one basket, and you will understand immediately why and how. I will refer you straight away to paragraph 38 of the indictment, which concerns killings. The Trial Chamber on the basis of Appendix C finds that there is no case to answer with regard to the killing of a number of people in -- I am quoting from the indictment -- "The killing of a number of people in the market place and surrounding area in Bosanska Gradiska town on or about August 1992, Bosanska Gradiska municipality." I see you taking notes, Mr. Ackerman, and probably you will be doing the same. At the end of the sitting, these notes that I have which are the basis of the oral decision, I will make them available to both of you so that it will make your life easier. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So in the meantime I will -- I will be able to maintain a constant speed. So in paragraph 38, the Trial Chamber finds that there is no case to answer with regard to the killing of these people in Bosanska Gradiska, as well as the killing of a number of people in the villages of Orasce and Duljci between the 20th and 23rd of September, 1992. This is in Bihac and Ripac municipality. As a consequence, a decision of acquittal is being taken with respect to these two incidents under counts 1, genocide; under count 2, complicity in genocide; 3, persecution because of the cross-reference that there is; 4, extermination because of the cross-reference that there is; and 5, wilful killings, as well because of the cross-reference that there is. And that's the first decision that we are taking.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- I'm sorry to interrupt. May I just for the purpose of the record make this clear. Your Honour is not acquitting Mr. Brdjanin of the count but merely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. But just for the purposes of the record. But merely striking from the indictment those examples which are not proved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As far as, for example, if we're taking count 5, wilful killings, in as far as there is pleaded that Mr. Brdjanin was responsible for the killing of these people in Bosanska Gradiska and the killing of the people in Orasce and Duljci, we are saying that there is no case to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The rest stays. And at the end of the day we will probably, as you may imagine, we will be calling upon you to put the indictment in a washing machine again and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we have. And I was going to raise that when Your Honour had finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we are more or less on the same wavelength already and it will make our life easier. Paragraph 40 of the indictment, which I refer you now. In paragraph 40, with reference to camps, the Trial Chamber finds that there is no case to answer with regard to the alleged camps and detention facilities staffed and operated by military and police personnel under the direction of the Crisis Staffs and the VRS at and solely at Bosanska Dubica municipality, SUP building, the SUP buildings, and Bihac-Ripac municipality, Traktorski Servis and Ripac. Consequently, the Trial Chamber is deciding in favour of acquittal as regards these two counts under counts 1, genocide; 2, complicity in genocide; 3, persecutions with regard to any incidents alleged to have occurred in either of these two camps. I refer you to paragraph 42 of the indictment. In paragraph 42 of the indictment, in the -- in the part dealing with causing bodily -- serious bodily harm or mental harm, the Trial Chamber finds that there is no case to answer with regard to the following events. And I am reading now from the indictment itself. Bihac and Ripac. "From 9 June 1992, the village of Ripac was sealed off and became a de facto centre of detention for the Bosnian Muslim inhabitants. A hangar (Traktorski Servis) was utilised as a detention facility for inhabitants and Bosnian Muslims from other areas. Some detainees were tied up, beatings took place outside and during interrogations when detainees were accused of being members of the 'Green Berets.' Detainees were subject to forced labour. All detainees were non-combatants." Bosanska Dubica. "Between 1 April 1992 and 30 September 1992, number of Bosnian Muslim non-combatants were detained by members of the Bosnian Serb authorities (police forces and military). They were taken to the police (SUP) building. Beatings, involving the use of fists, feet, batons, electric cables and rifle butts, were administered by members of the police, military police, and SDS. The beatings were both arbitrary and during interrogations, the object of which was to persuade detainees to confess to involvement in the activities of the SDA, a legitimate political party. Some detainees were rendered unconscious as a result and/or suffered serious injury. Beatings were witnessed by other detainees." Bosanska Gradiska. "After 15 July 1992, some Bosnian Muslim non-combatants were detained by the police, reserve police and military police at the school in Bistrica and the police station in Bosanska Gradiska. At Bistrica and the police station in Bosanska Gradiska detainees were interrogated, beaten, and tortured." As a result, the Trial Chamber acquits the accused under counts 1, genocide; 2, complicity in genocide; and 3, persecutions, with regard to the events just mentioned. With respect to counts 6 and 7, to which these events also refer - and we're talking of torture now - the Trial Chamber notes that paragraph 53 of the indictment re-alleges and re-incorporates the incidents in paragraph 42, including those alleged to have taken place in Bihac-Ripac, Bosanska Dubica, and Bosanska Gradiska. However, the Trial Chamber is not of the opinion that it needs to enter any decision of acquittal with respect to these incidents under these counts because they are not pleaded by the Prosecution in paragraph 55 as featuring the intentional infliction of severe pain or suffering on Bosnian Muslims or Bosnian Croats. Paragraph 47 of the indictment, to which I refer you now. The Trial Chamber has come to the conclusion with reference to this -- to paragraph 47(3)(a) that there is no case to answer to the charge of destruction, willful damage, and looting of the residential and commercial properties in the parts of towns, villages, and other areas inhabited predominantly by a Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat population in: The town of Ripac, Orasac, the town of Bosanska Dubica, the town of Bosanska Gradiska, Liskovac, Orahovo, in respect of which incidents the Trial Chamber is issuing a decision of acquittal under counts 3, persecutions; 10, unlawful and wanton destruction of and appropriation of property not justified by military necessity; and count 11, wanton destruction of cities, towns, or villages or devastation not justified by military necessity. They're always referring to paragraph 47 but a different part of paragraph 47. The Trial Chamber has come to the conclusion with reference to paragraph 47(3)(b) that there is no case to answer to the charge of destruction and willful damage to the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat religious and cultural buildings listed in part B of Appendix C to the Prosecution's response, subject to the following two qualifications, which I hope will be clarified within the next few minutes. I will not be reading out part B of Appendix C, because I don't think it would make sense. It is here, the list is here, you can actually refer to it later on when I -- when I give you this document. The first qualification or the first point I wanted to make is the following; that going through the list Judge Janu, Judge Taya, and myself noticed that Ljubija -- in Appendix C, the Prosecution refers to the alleged destruction, not proven, of Ljubija mosque, Ljubija mosque, in the Prijedor municipality. In reality, if you refer to the indictment itself, paragraph 47(3)(b) where it refers to Ljubija, it refers to the Ljubija Roman Catholic parish church. So there is an inconsistency because the indictment pleads Ljubija Roman Catholic Church and the Prosecution is saying that it has not brought forward evidence to prove the destruction of the mosque in Ljubija with which your client was not charged. I mean, there was no way we could contact either of you in the course of -- of our deliberations, because I don't believe that that should be done, so what we are doing is that once we are making you aware of this, we are sure that a solution is going to be found, and the matter will be addressed in the written decision but will not be addressed today. So while we are taking into consideration what you have stated in Appendix -- part B of Appendix C, Ms. Korner, and what is stated in the indictment we will reserve the decision until later when we hand down the written decision. And if you meant there is no case to answer with regard to the Catholic church -- Roman Catholic Church in Ljubija, we will issue a decision of acquittal with regard to that event. If you still intended mosque, we obviously are going to say that was never pleaded. So that's the position. The second matter arises from a comment that you yourself, Ms. Korner, made in part B of Appendix C, and that's with regard to Kljevci, which in the indictment is included under Sanski Most. And you note and you draw our attention to the fact that Kljevci does not -- is not in Sanski Most but in Prijedor municipality. So we have this problem. But as I was explaining earlier on, it doesn't bother us in the least because if it remains as it is, in other words Kljevci Roman Catholic church in Sanski Most, which does not exist because Kljevci does not exist in Sanski Most, it's not a problem because we will find a decision of no case to answer, a decision of acquittal. If it's in Prijedor, then it was not pleaded and your client does not have to worry about it. So that is the two matters that -- please help us clear up from our -- our desk within now -- between now and when we hand down the written -- the written decision. So basically the position is a decision of acquittal is being taken with results -- with respect to the incidents listed in part B of Appendix C to the Prosecution's response under counts 3, persecution; count 12, destruction or willful damage done to the institutions dedicated to religion, with the exception as stated of Ljubija mosque and -- or Ljubija Roman Catholic parish church. With regard to the other ones, as I said, we'll deal with it. I don't think there -- there is a problem. We can return a decision of acquittal irrespective of whether you choose to retain it under Sanski Most or whether you prefer us to put it under -- under Prijedor. Please stay with paragraph 47 of the indictment, and I refer you to paragraph 47(4). And the Trial Chamber, having considered the evidence using the Jelesic standard, comes to the conclusion that there is no case to answer to the charge of deportation or forcible transfer of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from areas within the ARK municipality listed in para 4 of the indictment to areas under the control of the legitimate government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, in respect and only in respect of the municipalities mentioned earlier, that is, Bihac-Ripac, Bosanska Dubica, and Bosanska Gradiska. In respect to any such incidents occurring in these three municipalities, the Trial Chamber correspondingly enters a decision of acquittal under counts 3, persecutions; 8, deportation; and 9, inhumane acts, forcible transfers. Always remaining in paragraph 47, but this time subpara 5 of that paragraph, the Trial Chamber, again using the same yardstick, the same standards, Jelesic, has come to the conclusion that there is no case to answer to the charge of the denial of fundamental rights to Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats, including the right to employment, freedom of movement, right to property -- proper judicial process, or right to proper medical care, in any of the municipalities mentioned earlier, that is, Bihac-Ripac, Bosanska Dubica, and Bosanska Gradiska. The Trial Chamber correspondingly and accordingly enters a decision of acquittal with regard to these -- with regard to this charge under count 3, persecutions, as it relates to these three municipalities. Now we come to another part of our decision, and that is -- relates to Appendix D, which was attached to the Prosecution's response. As you are aware, Mr. Ackerman, the Prosecution in Appendix D lists incidents for which, although not listed in the indictment, it submits that sufficient evidence has been provided such that a reasonable trier of fact could arrive at a conviction beyond reasonable doubt. The Prosecution states that "It has proved the damage or destruction of other religious buildings not listed in the indictment ... and will apply to amend the indictment accordingly." Leaving the motion to amend the indictment accordingly apart - we'll come to that later on at some point in time today - the Trial Chamber wants to make it clear that the decision to proceed or not -- or to proceed or not to acquit at this stage, when reached, is not and has not been based in any way on any of these events. We have specifically left them out from our considerations. The relative evidence is not at the moment excluded from the trial because decisions on a probative value of testimony will be taken at the end of the trial. There is nothing at this stage, however, to exclude this evidence on the basis of relevance. Obviously, the events listed in Appendix D, the merit of whatever is involved in the discussion on these events and on the submissions that have been made will be taken up at a later stage and at the appropriate moment. Now we come to individual responsibility of the accused. This is a specific area which we want to address today and which will obviously be addressed much more fully in the written decision. The Prosecution cumulatively charges Radoslav Brdjanin under different modes of liability. We are going to digress a little bit on this because we don't agree with one of the submissions that has been made by the Prosecution as to the way we should have conducted our exercise. So we don't agree, so we are -- we are stating it and more or less then you will understand why we have done this whole exercise. The Prosecution, as I said, cumulatively charges your client under different modes of liability, that is, the first responsibility for knowingly and willfully participating in a joint criminal enterprise which entails his individual responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Statute. And then the Prosecution also charges your client with responsibility under 7(1) of the Statute for having planned, instigated, ordered or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation, or execution of the crimes charged in the indictment. And lastly, the Prosecution charges your client with responsibility for the acts committed by his subordinates whilst he was holding a position of superior authority, pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute. In its response to the 98 bis motion, the Prosecution submitted that it was not necessary for the Trial Chamber to address particular modes of liability at the Rule 98 bis stage. We came to the conclusion that we could not agree with the Prosecution on this point, also because we came to the conclusion that one of the purposes of the Rule 98 bis motion is that if your client is left with a case to answer, then the position should be -- be presented in as clear a way as possible and not left in -- not have any particular important matter such as the modes of criminal responsibilities which he will have to answer at the end of this trial, left in a vacuum. We have, therefore, examined each of these modes of individual criminal responsibility using the Jelesic test to -- to apply them to the facts. And we start with the joint criminal responsibility. We are going to be very concise in this, but do expect an elaborate analogy of this in the written decision, because these parts, as you may imagine, engaged us considerably in our -- in our deliberations. The first point that we are going to make, which we wouldn't have made under normal circumstances, arises from the fact that both you, Mr. Ackerman, and you, Ms. Korner, dedicated what we consider substantial part of your elaborate motion and response, respectively, to the second category of joint criminal enterprise. While it was my impression from the very beginning when I started this trial, way back in January of 2002, that the second category of joint criminal enterprise was not being pleaded. You put me in doubt, to tell you the truth, both of you, because you were referring and also making pronouncements on what constitutes the second category, and we went back into the -- to look at the decisions that were taken by my predecessor, Judge Hunt, when he was Pre-Trial Judge in this case, and we have come to the conclusion that the submissions that you've both made, with regard to the second category of joint criminal enterprise - to be precise, we're talking of the concentration camp category - does -- does not have any relevance for the purpose of this trial because we cannot consider now at this stage that category 2, joint criminal enterprise, has been pleaded. So that is one decision that we have taken. With regard to joint criminal enterprise, one point which was raised by the Defence and which we have considered and which we are going to touch upon now, again more to be expected in the written decision, and this is -- we concur with the Defence in that the notion of genocide as a natural and foreseeable consequence of an enterprise, not aimed specifically at genocide, is not compatible with the definition of "genocide" under Article 4(3)(a) of the Statute because of the intent required under that subparagraph, which is specifically to "The intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group, as such." Accordingly, the Trial Chamber is dismissing count 1 in the context of the category 3 joint criminal enterprise case. We will expand on this in our -- in our written -- written decision. Brdjanin was also charged or has been charged also with -- under 7(1) of the Statute, and that's criminal individual responsibility, and the Trial Chamber is satisfied on a prima facie basis but within the parameters of the Jelesic decision that the evidence establishes Radoslav Brdjanin's responsibility pursuant to 7(1) of the Statute, that is for having planned, instigated, ordered, or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation, or execution of the crimes charged under counts 1 through 12 of the indictment. In other words, I'm not again repeating each time the words of Jelesic, the conclusion is that a reasonable trier of fact would come to a conclusion of conviction. With regard to Article 7(3), we also are satisfied on the same prima facie basis but within the parameters of the Jelesic judgement that the evidence sufficiently establishes Radoslav Brdjanin's responsibility pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute for crimes charged under counts 1 through 12 of the indictment. And we are now going to tackle two further points only, and we come to the conclusion. And the first one relates to genocide. In its response, the Prosecution submits -- the reference you will find in the written decision. I mean, I don't have reference to paragraphs here. But in its response, the Prosecution submits that "The mass deportation of Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat groups" constitutes conditions of life calculated to bring about their physical destruction, within the meaning of Article 4(2)(c) of the Statute. It may well be so, but the Trial Chamber does not entertain this submission, will not accept it, for the reason that this is not pleaded in the indictment, as paragraphs 37 -- as reference to paragraphs 37(3) and 43 of the indictment will clearly show. The last point is with regard to extermination. The Trial Chamber is grateful for the submissions made by both the Defence in its motion and the -- the Prosecution in its elaborate response. And with regard to extermination would like to point out that after due consideration to case law and also your submissions and also authors and doctrine, we accept as the correct legal approach the formulation of the mens rea element with regard to extermination as explained in the Vasiljevic trial judgement, that is, the mens rea comprising the requirement to prove that your client "had knowledge that his action is part of a vast murderous enterprise in which a large number of individuals are systematically marked for killing or were killed." The Trial Chamber is aware that there are at least two other judgements (Krstic and Stakic) which differ from the Vasiljevic approach. All three cases are currently pending before the Appeals Chamber. For the purpose of this Rule 98 bis exercise, the Trial Chamber chose to apply the pronouncement which is more favourable to the accused, namely that found in the Vasiljevic trial judgement, and leaves the matter to be definitively decided in a later stage, hopefully after a decision of the Appeals Chamber. Our conclusion, therefore, saving all that has already been decided, with regard to the various counts and various incidents or events, the Trial Chamber dismisses the remainder of the accused's motion on the basis that it is the conviction of this Trial Chamber that there is sufficient evidence, which if accepted, upon which -- if accepted, upon which a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused on the relevant particular charges. As I said, this is not an official document. Please don't treat it as official. I'm just giving you a copy to make things easier for you. Chuqing, if you can hand this over. And there are verbal additions that I have made, as you can imagine, qualifications here and qualifications there. So I don't expect anyone to take advantage of the document at a later point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think we're both aware that it's the actual written judgement, as Your Honour said, that will be the deciding factor. Your Honour, subject to anything Your Honours may say about this, it seems to me that the logical thing now would be for me to apply to Your Honours to have the indictment accepted which we submitted in our addendum. Your Honour, in that -- we haven't had it signed yet. I've never understood why in fact an indictment, which is a result of Your Honours' ruling, should have to be signed by the Prosecutor, but I think it has to. So there was a draft --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I know it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I stand to be corrected, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I think that's right. But we, therefore, appended to our addendum filed on the 16th of September a draft indictment which we would be proposing to lodge with the Court but which also includes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- the extra effectively religious buildings. Your Honour, may I just say this: They were proved through the evidence. They could remain simply in the evidence as similar fact evidence, but we thought it right that if at the end of the day there should be any sort of a conviction, that Mr. Brdjanin and the public should know exactly on what he had been convicted and so we applied to put those names into the indictment. May I say it is entirely a matter for Your Honours, but we felt that was the proper way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I think the matter can be addressed under two headings. One is the cleaning of the indictment, now taking into consideration the extraction from it of certain events, and particularly paragraph 4 of the indictment, which lists the municipalities and to which reference is made in various other parts of the indictment. But that can be done, and I think it has been done, and I don't think that should be -- should present any problem. If anything, it would -- it would help our work now and in the future. The second part is something which is completely different; that is, the Prosecution is applying to have included in the indictment under certain counts only reference to events, particularly destruction of religious and cultural, whatever, which were not included before. In other words, you will have a situation whereby the original list will first be shortened and then be lengthened again. So this is -- this is the proposal. Now, what's your position on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to -- I have no objection to the indictment being modified to conform to the judgement that you are entering. I do object to the indictment being amended to include matters that were not in the original indictment as to which there would have been no motivation for us to conduct cross-examination of any of the witnesses regarding those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are fully aware --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in fact, we could very well have been cut off by the Court had we gone into those because they weren't in the indictment, so I think it's totally unfair to now put them in the indictment when we can't contest them by cross-examination of the witness. If they're going to play any part in this case, it ought to be similar fact evidence, as suggested by Ms. Korner, but not a part of the indictment. I think that would be improper and unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in response, all I -- can I say this, that if there had been any dispute as to these matters, whether or not they were in the indictment, Mr. Ackerman would still have been under an obligation to cross-examine. As we now know from Mr. Ackerman's response, there is no dispute at all to any of what has -- I think we've been generally calling the basic, the evidence of basic crimes. I don't, therefore, see how Mr. Ackerman is in any way prejudiced. May I say this would happen in most jurisdictions, but this happened particularly in the Stakic case when Judge Schomburg himself said this was the proper way of doing things, that people who had been listed as killed at the back of the indictment, not proved were removed but those that had been -- the names of those proved but not listed were added. But Your Honour, as I say, I don't advocate strongly for this. If Your Honour feels that's an objection with merit, then so be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You both have strong points, actually. But I consider yours to be stronger than Mr. Ackerman's for a -- for a very simple reason, that although it is true that I would have stood up and repeated what you said; in other words, knowing that mosques and churches were coming out during examination-in-chief that were not included in the indictment, I didn't think it was appropriate or necessary to -- to cross-examine the witness upon. That would have made a hell of a lot of sense. But does it make sense any further or any more now, considering what Ms. Korner has stated, namely that as far as the facts are concerned, more or less you are not contesting that a number of churches, a number of mosques, a number of -- were burnt down? Does it really make a difference if instead of having -- I don't know, I haven't counted them -- but instead of having 10, you have 20? And in circumstances in which certainly there is not even a hint that your client was personally involved in the destruction of -- of these mosques or churches?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to make something very clear, because it appears to -- to not be very clear. But I thought I made it very clear in my motion. By my not contesting certain factual matters, I said I think very clearly in the motion that for the purposes of the motion I would not be contesting those matters but I was not making any admissions that the Prosecution has proven any of those factual matters beyond a reasonable doubt. And I want to make that very clear. I've not done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's how we understood it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've said for purposes of the motion the Trial Chamber can't consider these matters have been proven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what we understood, Mr. Ackerman. But does it really make a difference? Because these will be in the same block as -- as the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it only makes a difference, perhaps, Your Honour, with regard to sentencing. I mean, I can see a judge saying we're going to sentence the defendant 15 minutes for every mosque, or something, and if you add the mosques, then you have the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, this is not a case of willful destruction of property that you would have in a domestic jurisdiction which stands on its own. And if you've -- you've burnt down one barn, it's one way, if you have burnt an entire village it's another. It's -- you know, I don't think the case rests on the number of mosques that were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it's my job to state my position and your job to -- to decide the matter, so please go ahead and decide it and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, we are not --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- whatever you wish to decide is your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not exactly that keen either on -- on opening up the -- in the indictment. I mean, because I think even from the few words that I said in the oral decision, we made our position very clear that we do not intend to take them out of the evidence, definitely not. Because we all know that they ought to be there and they are relevant and they can have a probative value which can be assigned to them at a later stage. Whether -- whether the Tribunal is going to be convinced more that there was destruction of mosques and churches, religious -- religious buildings because there are, there are 30 instead of 20, I mean, I -- I will -- I am not prepared to commit myself. But on the other hand, I mean, it's self-explanatory if we had doubt as to whether a case where -- where just one mosque was destroyed or not, it's one thing. But here we have a number of mosques which have either been destroyed or not. And whether it was a systematic thing happening or whether it was just a sporadic incident which had no connotation with the rest of the case. Anyway, is that your position? Do you need -- do you want to add anything to what has been submitted? All right. We will discuss this amongst ourselves. We have discussed it already, you know, and -- but we came to the courtroom very much open to conviction from either side on this, and we take stock of what has been submitted and will -- will let you know what our decision will be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, I don't think it's possible. It's simply that we can get the new indictment, however it's formed, signed tomorrow and have it properly filed. At the moment it's been filed confidentially because we need Your Honours' rulings first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So perhaps -- I mean, I know there's going to have to be a break, I think, in what, half an hour or so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. We started --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What time did we sit? 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We started at about quarter to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So half an hour, yes. So if Your Honours were able to, after the break, perhaps let us know, that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Can we move to the pre-Defence conference? So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One thing. Your Honour, I'm sorry about that, those two aspects of confusion in our list in Annex B. We'll check that and get back to Your Honours over whether it's mosques or Catholic churches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Please do. I mean, no hurry. Because it's -- the written decision won't be available before a couple of weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can certainly, if that's all right, we can perhaps just file very quickly a supplementary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, let's start with the Pre-Defence Conference. And I've discussed this with my two colleagues and particularly with the staff. There was -- I'm referring to BT106.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we can even discuss BT--

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go perhaps into private session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to suggest that we need to lift the confidentiality of the first document that you had filed on the 1st of -- or the 4th of September. That's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I ask that we go into private session and perhaps we'll just elaborate slightly on what Your Honour is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. So it's the decision of this Trial Chamber to lift the confidentiality of its confidential decision reached -- or filed on the 4th of September, 2003 on the Prosecution's application to present new evidence. Arising from that, there was a motion subsequently on which I understand there was agreement reached between the two parties to delay the testimony of BT106 because of Mr. Cunningham not being able to be here when we had scheduled the hearing of BT106 to which the previous decision refers. And that's why we had to lift the confidentiality, because otherwise I wouldn't have been able to mention it. I just want a confirmation from you that the agreement that you reached and we were informed of still stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Mr. Ackerman has got something to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have filed today - and you obviously have not received it yet - a motion to either prohibit this witness from testifying at all or moving the testimony to the Prosecution's rebuttal case. And the basis of that motion is just today we were given a fairly large quantity of Rule 68 material regarding this witness that is all in B/C/S, untranslated. Mr. Cunningham has left the country. I can't imagine how we could be prepared to cross-examine this witness by Friday of next week with this kind of a situation. And I think it's more than just -- than just what meets the eye right now. This is all material that has been in the possession of the Prosecution for a very long period of time. And I will not stand here and accuse the Prosecutor of deliberately doing it this way, but it's -- I will say that it's a bit suspicious and certainly puts us in a position where in effect we're being denied the opportunity to fully cross-examine this witness by -- by this kind of a procedure. And I can go into greater detail about the material that was given us, Your Honour, if you'd like, and you will -- as soon as you know, you will recognise that it's material that has been around for a very long time, and we just found it in our box this -- this very morning. So that's where we are. But I have filed the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's all news to us. We -- we are not aware of the motion. We are not aware of the information that -- on which you back your motion. What's the position, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't aware of the motion until Mr. Ackerman came into court, just before Your Honours came in this afternoon. As far as I am aware, we disclosed on the 24th of September, and we're now, whatever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Today is the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The 9th of October. Now, may I say I appreciate straight away that Mr. Ackerman, I know, has been out of the country. I don't know where Mr. Cunningham has been. And what was disclosed today is -- is something different. But it was -- it's effectively statements which relate to the -- the matters that this witness is going to testify about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm more interested at this point in time at the real problem, because is it -- is it correct -- I mean, I don't doubt Mr. Ackerman's -- but I just want a confirmation of it. Is it correct that these documents that have been disclosed to -- to the Defence are in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Some are, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just hand the disclosure to you so you can see what it is?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that today's or the 24 of September?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I'm not complaining about 24 September. I'm complaining about 8 October, that we received this morning. That's the only thing that I'm complaining about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think -- in that case, I think, Mr. Ackerman, you'll find it's got nothing to do with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It claims to have everything to do with the witness. Now, maybe I'm -- maybe I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as I know, it's to do with -- I wonder if I -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, we haven't got the disclosure here, because I wasn't aware this was going to be raised. I wonder if I can see what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Let's have a look at it, Mr. Ackerman. At least we'll have an indication of what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't -- since I can't read them, I can't be certain, but, you know, maybe what Ms. Korner said is correct. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But they obviously have a reference number. Through the reference number Ms. Gustin can find out what they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only thing that relates to Witness 106 is in English, which is a list of points relating -- which we -- Your Honours ordered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The remainder of the stuff, which is in B/C/S, relates to witnesses that Mr. Ackerman intends apparently to call. If he looks at the first document, it's an intercept between Vojo Kupresanin and others. We felt that as we now were notified of witnesses that Mr. Ackerman wanted to call, if we had documents which related to those witnesses, which hadn't been disclosed to him, they should be disclosed and that's what the letter says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We can -- we can cut it short, Your Honour. I've obviously misapprehended. I assume that all of those documents that were in B/C/S contained within them information regarding that witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so I apologise to the Court for labouring you all with this matter and the motion will be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And us? What about us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] So going back now to square 1. I was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honours, getting, back to what Your Honours asked, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we're all agreed. There's no problem the witness will testify after the cross-examination of Mr. Brown and Mr. Trainer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do you agree, Mr. Ackerman? Okay. So there's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As long as, Your Honour, it's within the time frame of Mr. Cunningham's return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay. But I don't think you are going to find us trying to extract blood. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I don't think there is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Before we leave that witness, can I go back into private session for one moment? Because there is one matter I want to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, we are now going to proceed with the Pre-Defence Conference, which is being convened pursuant to Rule 73 ter. And there are a few notes that -- or points that I need to note. The first one relates to our scheduling order of the 31st of July and the Rule 65 ter -- With reference to Rule 65 ter, the Defence filed on the 23rd of September the confidential submission pursuant to Rule 65 ter. Subsequently we had, or at least we were informed that Mr. Ackerman wanted to file -- or to present a revised witness list. I gave instructions to the -- my legal officer -- to the legal officer of Trial Chamber II to request from -- require from Mr. Ackerman a proper formal filing, which we got today. We were not -- because I specifically refused to have in -- accept an unofficial list, so the second list that we have been able to look at is the one which arrived today, with which you filed this morning. In the short time available, I have tried to compare and contrast the two documents, but perhaps you would be in a position to explain that better yourself, Mr. Ackerman, when we come to that stage. We obviously will need to refer now to the revised list, which is comprehensive of the first one. I note, or at least until I received this, I had noted that in the previous one you had failed, Mr. Ackerman, to name any of the four expert witnesses listed. And I think at least with regard to two of them as they appear on the last page of the revised, we are still in the same position, number 61 and 62.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're now utterly confused, because we don't know anything about anything being filed today. We were sent an e-mail by -- or either -- today by Mr. Ackerman, including a -- what to us is the third version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is -- this is supposed to be the third, I think, version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So this is the one that's been filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me try and explain it. There was a first version which was filed ahead of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- time, for which I'm thankful, because it gave us an idea of what to expect on -- on a broad basis. Then I was informed by one of my legal staff that Mr. Ackerman had handed another list, was not intending to file it officially as it was a revised list, and I said -- I told my legal officer, "Please tell Mr. Ackerman that I insist upon having it filed officially and until there is an official addendum or revised list, I will not look at any list that he may have handed to you." I was also informed that he handed the same list, an unofficial list, to the Prosecution. So that much I was informed. I know that my staff was trying to get in touch with Mr. Ackerman, and at least one of my staff got in touch with Mr. Ackerman yesterday evening, I suppose, yesterday. And I was informed this morning to expect a revised list, which arrived at about half past 1.00 this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I just want to check it's the same that we were sent. I imagine it is. But it contains no names of any experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. In fact, that is -- I am starting with that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- because it's one thing that we need to clarify, not necessarily today but we can't leave it pending just like that. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness list that -- that was filed today has in the -- on the first page in the upper left-hand corner, "Rev. 8/10/03." That's the one that was sent to you at the same time it was filed. So you will also get a filing along with that, Ms. Korner. With regard to expert witnesses, Your Honour, I'll be providing those as soon as possible. We're still in negotiations with -- with at least two of them, and we're not absolutely certain whether or not they're going to accept the terms that the Registry is willing to extend. And so we're involved in that. But I would expect fairly soon that we will have those names. We do not intend to call any expert witness until very near the end of the Defence case, so I think we're looking at -- at January before we actually call an expert witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we've made two points.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say that I -- that was one of the points that I wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honours prefer to go through yours and then I'll come back to this? Because otherwise, I want to make a point about what's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am pretty sure that what you have jotted down as points will -- will overlap with -- probably with mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's proceed. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But let's make these two points first: Number one, Mr. Ackerman is stating that the -- the expert witnesses will be brought forward towards the end of his case and that he will -- he undertakes to submit the names of these witnesses ASAP after finalising with them the terms under which they can testify.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I understand that. But he says two out of the four. Therefore, can I take it there are two where he has the experts' names, if not the full reports? Your Honour, I'm not quarrelling, and indeed I couldn't, because our experts reports came late on. But Mr. Ackerman knew from the beginning whom our experts were going to be. I'm asking for the names of those that he has definitely decided to call. And Your Honour, I'll make it absolutely clear, so we can commence our researches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I would ask to make an order that the names of the two that he says that he's still in negotiation with should be provided if they're to be called within the next 14 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The experts feature, or at least what I can see from this revised list, under 59, 60, 61 and 62. Correct me if I'm wrong, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, in none of these cases do we have an indication of who you intend to submit as an expert? Only the area of expertise that they would --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct right now. But I will supply -- I think I can supply at least two names within 24, 48 hours, something like that. Then the rest are going to take a little longer. And if -- if the two people who we're negotiating with say no, then we have to start searching for someone else. But we're hoping they'll both accept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which two are you referring to? Which areas of expertise?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Military and police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So can I take it the constitutional law expert has been chosen? And if so, could I have his name? And Your Honour, in respect of graphology, it doesn't say to what area. Is this towards Mr. Brdjanin's signature or to Rasula's diary or to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the graphology, the handwriting expert, you'll recall that during the testimony of several witnesses we got signatures from the witness to compare with signatures that were contended to be theirs in various documents. There are, I think, three of those. And that's what that witness will be testifying about. I would tell you the name right now, but I've forgotten it. I will -- I will get it -- I will get it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the point raised by Ms. Korner is perfectly legitimate, because -- in fact, I was -- I was coming to one what -- I'm going to use the word "shortcoming" because technically it is a shortcoming. But you did not as such follow the requirements of our scheduling order and what is required by the Rules themselves. And that is not only a short summary of what the witness intends to testify upon, but supposedly you were also supposed to specify on the witness list the points in the indictment as to which each witness will testify and you haven't -- you haven't done this. Also, I could mention that some of the summaries are not summaries at all, just a very, very, very skimpy indication of what could possibly be the -- the subject matter of -- of the testimony, but not even a summary. So I think we need to dwell on this a little bit, dwell on this a little bit, and with regard to the experts in particular because, as you know, the -- the Rules provide for a time limit reserved for the other party. Now, it's true that the other party may -- may renounce to that time limit, but the fact that there is a time limit could create problems if you delay the disclosure of the names in particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I, I think -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. But can I just stick for a moment to the expert. Your Honour, it may well be that we're going to object to this, the graphology stuff on the basis of relevance and peripheral issues, but until I see a report it's very difficult. But I would like to know -- we've drifted slightly away. What is the name, please, of the constitutional expert? Apparently Mr. Ackerman have some kind of report and does know who it is, because he's saying it's the military and police he's still negotiating with. So could we be told who it is, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to try to supply the name within 48 hours, and I'll do that. Again, I'm not going to supply it here in open court. And let me say this in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In some defence. No, not in private session either, because we're not completely finished yet. And again, I don't know the name off the top of my head. But it's -- I'm not trying to keep it from the Prosecution. Please understand, that's not what I'm doing. But let me say this in defence of what we've done at this point: There has not been a moment since we last left here that I sat around wondering what maybe I should do next. We were given insufficient time to prepare the Defence, in my view. We have spent -- we have worked extraordinarily hard trying to get just to where we've gotten. And I can just tell you that we are -- we're willing to start calling witnesses when you ask us to start calling witnesses, but we're not ready. And we haven't completed all the work that needed to be done. We have a very small staff. We don't have a staff like the Prosecutor has. We have been working extraordinarily hard, every one of us, and people who are volunteers who are not be paid are working to try to help us get to the point we need to get to cooperate with this Chamber to try to get this case going on the schedule that you want it to go on. We're doing everything we can to make that happen. We have spent on extraordinary amount of time in Bosnia recently working very hard to try to get there. And so it's not that we're sitting around not doing things that we should be doing. It's that we haven't had time to do the things that we should be doing and we recognise that. But, you know, we haven't been given sufficient time to prepare this Defence. We asked for it. It was denied. So we're doing the best we can on the time schedule that you want us to be on, Your Honour. And we're not complaining all that much about it. We just need the -- the Chamber to understand that it's not as elegant as we would like it to be in terms of what we're able to -- to provide. We're not hiding anything from anybody, not trying to hide anything from anybody. We're doing as good a job as I think we can do under the circumstances, and that's what I want to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's, again, back to the -- to the two experts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say, I'm asking Your Honour to order Mr. Ackerman to tell us the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the two of them I'm going to order Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- to give us the name within 48 hours. It should be enough time to refresh your memory, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can do it as soon as I get back to my flat, Your Honour. I just can't do it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So -- no, I understand that. I mean, I'm absolutely hopeless when it comes to names myself, so I'm not surprised. That's number one. The other two --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have some issues to raise, but I note the time, on this --

utterances.text: The other --

utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not the one that's deciding. It's the -- it's the witnesses that are deciding.
