utterances.text: I know. But if you want me to impose it, I will impose it. But it's not my style to impose it if the Defence can help itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The -- I don't know how to explain. One of the witnesses, for instance, we have been communicating almost exclusively by e-mail. Mr. Cunningham will personally contact him tomorrow, and we may have an answer as early as tomorrow, but I don't know. And until I know, it makes no sense for me to say and to make some pronouncement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The other, we're still waiting for information from Bosnia regarding the other person, and we should have that, I hope, rather soon, Your Honour. I'm expecting that within three or four days, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's the sitting of optimism today. I mean, everyone is very hopeful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I think -- I'm very hopeful, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm going to set a time limit as soon as we start again after the break. In the meantime, we'll have a 20-minute break, and we will also come out with a decision on the amendment -- suggested or proposed amended indictment. Thank you. Twenty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Brdjanin is here, Mr. Ackerman and Ms. Korner are here. So two decisions. Decision number 1: With regard to the addendum -- let me refer to it -- we are now back, technically speaking, so that we will keep it at that -- the first part of this -- today's hearing was a trial day proper, because we -- we were handing down a decision. Arising out of that, we need to give a second decision, which we are going to give now, so we are reconvened for the purpose of this decision as the Trial Chamber during trial. All right? And this is the second decision that we are handing down, relating to the addendum to the Prosecutor's response to the motion for judgement of acquittal, Rule 98 bis, filed on the 16th of September. We have taken due consideration -- into consideration the respective submissions made by the Prosecution and the Defence. As we stated earlier, we see value to -- in both, but I think in the interest of a fair trial will be secured better if at the stage of the proceedings the request of the Prosecution is to have the indictment amended by the inclusion of the events mentioned in Appendix D to the response - I've lost track now - if the request is turned down, and we are actually turning down the request. The indictment will be adjusted accordingly to reflect also the decision that we are -- we took earlier with regard to the Rule 98 bis, but I think we have come -- not I think; we have come to the conclusion that in fairness -- for fairness sake, the evidence remains there. What importance we attach to it will depend later on -- according to what we will decide. But there's not going to be an amended indictment to include those. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, in that case, we'll -- we'll -- the indictment that we produce for signature which we filed will be one that merely takes into account Your Honours' rulings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. Yes, please. Thank you. That's number 1. Number 2: We are now reconvened in the Pre-Defence Conference. And the trial sitting hearing stands adjourned until Monday, the 13th. Correct? Correct me if I'm wrong. Monday, the 13th we start. No? Monday, the 13th. So we start with the Pre-Trial -- the Pre-Defence Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First, Mr. Ackerman, you have until Monday to disclose the names of the experts you intend to produce under 59 as expert in graphology and under 60 as constitutional law expert. And the Trial Chamber has recorded what Ms. Korner said earlier with regard to the possibility of challenging the expert in graphology. But that's something that we will come to later. With regard to the military expert and police expert, we appreciate that you, as you said, Mr. Ackerman, you have encountered problems there. We also appreciate that you are optimistic that this matter can be solved shortly. So tentatively we are giving a date -- a maximum date of ten days from today, and then we'll take it up from there. In these ten days, please make an effort like you have done in the past to fill in these blanks. Ms. Korner, I am going to take your advice and hand over to you so that you can deal or raise the matters that you have in your mind on what we need to do and how we need to proceed. And then we'll go back ourselves to what we have here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm so sorry that you thought it was advice. I was merely seeking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It's -- I take it as an advice too. Why not? I mean, it's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I deal with what is completely absent from any filing by Mr. Ackerman. The Rule 65(G)(i) -- (ii) is the list -- well, can I come back to (i). But (ii), a list of exhibits the Defence intends to offer. I can start with that? There's a complete lack of -- of any exhibits. The Defence invoked reciprocal disclosure and we had a couple of disclosures - and by "a couple" I'll not saying it may not have been more than two, but it wasn't very many - which for the most part merely returned to us our documents that we had disclosed to him. So my first request for Your Honours to make a ruling on is that we receive from the Defence a list of exhibits that they intend to use with witnesses, in the plural. In particular, if there are any documents to be produced through witnesses which have not been disclosed to us before - and by that I mean documents which we ourselves didn't disclose to the Defence - that that be provided to us before the Defence case actually starts on the 13th -- on -- no, the 20th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. This also -- was also one point that I had made here: "The Defence has failed to file the following: List of exhibits the Defence intends to offer in its case stating, where possible, whether the Prosecutor has any objection as to authenticity," which is wishful thinking at the present moment because we don't even have the list. That's number one. "In addition, copies of the exhibits so listed have to be served on the Prosecution." And I had intended to ask both of you to -- to enlighten us on this matter, because there may be a reason for not having the list now, which I'm sure is going to be that we never gave you enough time, Mr. Ackerman, to prepare your Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I haven't had enough time to put the list together, Your Honour. And I -- if you ask me to identify one exhibit right now that I'm going to use in the defence that I have not given to the Prosecutor, I don't think I'd be able to do so. But that's kind of the next thing on our list of -- of something to concentrate on rather heavily. We do have documents, many of them have already been turned over to the Prosecution, but I -- I just need to find the time and -- and the people to sit down with the rest of those documents and see what of those documents we really need to -- to use. I have sent off a couple of -- of requests to -- to some people previously associated with the case just asking them out of the kindness of their heart to assist me with this, even though they won't be paid a cent for doing it. And because they're very familiar with the documents and -- and I'm just doing this as rapid as I can. But I think I can have that list to the Prosecutor and to Your Honours before -- before too much longer. Now, whether -- whether I'll be able to supply the Prosecution with every document I intend to use with every witness by the time we open our case on Monday, that's -- that's virtually impossible. But I can tell you that we will operate just as conscientiously as the Prosecutor did. We will sometimes bring a document in the day we intend to use it; sometimes we'll supply it two days before, which is what the Prosecutor did throughout their case. I don't think we should be held to any higher standard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what he -- was left for him to say was, "Honourable Judges, what's good for the goose is also good for the gander." So, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, we've had this goose versus the gander syndrome before. But I would remind Your Honours that the only time that documents were produced on the day that the witness was testifying was when the witness suddenly arrived with a document. I'm not -- I appreciate, of course, that this is going to happen. What I'm asking for, first of all, is a list with a description of the documents that it is intended to use for the witnesses. I'm then asking that in due time for the particular witnesses called and particularly where -- and by "new" I mean documents that were not disclosed to us to Mr. Ackerman. I mean a witness who's going to come forward with -- and wouldn't be it wonderful, for example, the minutes of the ARK Crisis Staff meetings. That is something -- a document like that, which is clearly relevant and important, then there will be an objection, Your Honour, and it's going to slow the proceedings down because we're going to have to make inquiries about it. So, Your Honour, all of this is designed, firstly, that there should be fair trial all round; that there shouldn't be a trial by ambush; and third, that there should be as little delay to the trial as possible. So I'm asking at the moment, Your Honour, that -- for a simple order that by the 20th of October we are given a list. I'm asking at the moment for copies, and we'll see how we go from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you live with that, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'll do my best. I -- I really want -- I just -- I want it to be very clearly understood as much by -- by Ms. Korner as by the Trial Chamber that the last thing in the world that I will do is withhold a document for tactical reasons just to -- to drive the Prosecution crazy and make life difficult --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation Continues] ... if I catch you doing that, Mr. Ackerman, you will be in serious trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I should be. And I wouldn't do that and I will not do that. I'm going to provide things to the Prosecution as soon as I know what I'm going to do with them; they'll be the first people to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But unfortunately we cannot continue using such descriptions as "as soon as" or -- let's fix a date. It has been suggested for the handing over of a list 20th of October. You should have at least a provisional list provided by that day. Today is only the 9th. Mr. Ackerman. It's a Monday. It's not -- the 20th is a Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you have two weekends.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless you're going back to Yugoslavia or to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's me and Mr. Vujic. Mr. Cunningham is in court in the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he will be back when -- he will be back next week, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, he'll be back next week. We have two rather complicated expert witnesses to cross-examine. We have another complicated witness for Mr. Cunningham to cross-examine. We can stop preparing for those witnesses and put together this witness list, which seems to me an extraordinarily foolish thing to do. If you say the 20th, we'll come up with some kind of a list on the 20th, but it's going to be -- it's going to be as good as we can do at that point. I can't guarantee that it's going to be -- I can't make it any better than I can make it. I'll do the best I can, that's all I can tell you; I'll do the best I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you're forcing my hands because -- you know, I mean, I -- I will be the first one to be criticised if I allow proceedings to go on with, you know, along these lines. Yes, let's see and let's see and -- I am supposed to establish a deadline.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to establish a deadline if you can come forward and tell me, "Judge, by the 20th you will all have a list."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know, it would help a great deal if this Tribunal would honour the commitment to equality of arms. It refuses to do so. The Prosecutor has a huge staff; you order them to produce a list by the 20th, they can put 15 people to work on it and do it. I can put one person to work on it, maybe two if I'm lucky, because I don't get equality of arms. I don't get the staff that I need. I'm never given the staff that I need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- and that's not fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- you haven't come into this case now. You've been in this case for two years plus.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With the same limited staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would never believe you or take you seriously if you were to stand up and tell me, "Judge, I don't know what documents to -- I will be -- exhibits I will be intending to offer." Maybe you haven't organised them in a list, but I'm pretty sure you know exactly what documents -- or at least the majority of exhibits that you will be --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do not, and that's why I'm telling you'll that's how well I can do this. I may have 100 documents, 20 of which I'm going to use, but I'm not sure which 20 yet. I may have 240 that I'm going to use. I can't tell you that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But that puts you in the same position as the Prosecution. And then with the Prosecution we have always had a situation from one month to the -- to the next of having initially a big binder or a big folder of documents intended to be tendered and then we end up with maybe -- maybe two or three or five per cent of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm never in the same position as the Prosecution, never, because this Tribunal will not recognise the concept of equality of arms and will not supply the Defence with the kind of resources necessary to accomplish our task. Right now we have a bunch of documents that we might want to use that are sitting with a translator that was approved by the Registrar to do translations for us in Banja Luka who they haven't paid yet this year and she has said, "I'm sorry, I can't work any longer for you. I have to do paying work." They haven't paid her once this year yet, so she has to quit. So we've got a stack of documents there that we can't get translated. We run into these kind of problems all the time. Our investigators are limited in hours. We asked them to do a task and they can't do it or if they do it, they don't get paid for it. We have enormous problems that the Prosecution never faces because of the lack of equality of arms. And now to say that we must perform at a higher level than what is expected of the Prosecution is just unfair. But I'll tell you that I will do everything I can and I will work almost non-stop to get it done. I will insist on sleeping a little bit, but that's about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, the date -- let's work this out first, because we have the Rules and I have to stick to the Rules to start with. I cannot create Rules myself. The case -- the Defence case officially starts when? On the 12th we have got --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Defence case starts on the 20th, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is the Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Unless the next week's witnesses run into the Monday, but otherwise it's the Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because -- because 65 ter (G), Mr. Ackerman, doesn't leave me any options. It doesn't also say that the list of exhibits will be the one and only that you will offer or that it cannot be changed or that you will be bound by it due and thus. There is the possibility, but the Rule is very specific, that this has to be filed before the commencement of the Defence case. So we'll -- I am going to establish the 20th as the day -- the time limit by which you -- you are to file this list of exhibits with the understanding that we all appreciate that this may not be the final list, that that would be subject to alterations, to amendments. At the same time, I do need to draw your attention to the fact that according to the second paragraph of 65 ter (G), then you are expected also to serve on the Prosecutor copies of the exhibits. So -- which shouldn't be difficult once you have established at least which -- which documents you're going to -- which exhibits you intend to offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there -- there will be a list as of that date, and there's no reason not to serve copies at the same time we produce the list. I mean, that -- that doesn't make any sense. So I'll certainly serve the copies at the same time I produce the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that solves temporarily at least the problem. Basically, for the record, the -- the attention of the Defence was drawn to the fact that a list of exhibits the Defence intends to offer in its case as requested by Rule 65 ter (G)(ii) has not been filed and the Trial Chamber is establishing a deadline for the filing of this list, the 20th -- the 20th of October, Monday, the 20th of October. And then we'll see from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want to make it clear to Your Honours and for the record that there are a large number of documents that are in the translation process, either with CLSS or with the person in Banja Luka who's not working now, that -- that might very well, in fact, very likely, will become exhibits, but I cannot make that determination until I can actually read the translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Ackerman. Incidentally, while we are on this point, have you brought up the matter of this translator or interpreter in Banja Luka not paid being by the Registry with the Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Two weeks ago I resubmitted her invoices with a note saying: "These invoices have not received any attention. Please give them some attention." Two weeks has gone by and nothing has happened. I sent another memo today saying, "Please look into this. Tell me what's going on with this, because she's stopped doing translations. Other people are paying her to translate, so she's doing their work instead of ours." And so that's where I've gotten so far. And I haven't gotten a reply back. That was a memo that I just sent today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I will check this -- this with the Registrar myself as well. From my experience, the Registrar gives these matters its utmost attention, and I'll see whether there is a particular reason, as sometimes there is, why this matter is being protracted. In which case, if it is a matter which is reserved to the Registrar, I will certainly not get involved, and please don't expect me to get involved. Yes. Before we move to the estimated length of Defence case, number of witnesses, et cetera, is there anything else you would like to raise, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Your Honour, there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour will see in the -- I'm now referring to the last filed list of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dates of birth appear for some but not for most. The reason that we asked for the dates of birth, as I made clear to Your Honour, I think, before we broke, is that in order to conduct meaningful searches of documents which relate, or statements which relate to these witnesses, so that if there's anything which may assist Your Honours in assessing these witnesses which we are in possession of can be made. Your Honour, I would like the dates of birth of these witnesses for whom they have not been supplied. And Your Honour, the first question almost of any investigator taking a statement from a witness will ask is, What is your date of birth? Or potential witness. And Your Honour, that must be, I would submit, in the possession of Mr. Ackerman or his investigators but has not been supplied. I don't know why. Your Honour, the adequacy of the summaries is a matter which Your Honours have already touched upon. It is simply not enough to say, for example, if I can take Your Honours to number 40, on the list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, don't mention names.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not going to. I'm going to mention numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. Because the list is confidential still, you know, because of obvious reasons. Yes, 40. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That tells you absolutely nothing at all. The actions of paramilitary formations in Teslic in the arrest and detention. Was he part of a formation? What exactly is he going to be saying? Number 42, who will testify about inter-ethnic relations in the relevant time period. We can get guess as to where he's coming from. It actually says it above there. But nonetheless, Your Honour, it's simply inadequate. And can I say I know that Mr. Ackerman can do better, because in respect of the -- can I take Your Honours to witnesses number 50 and number 55. Your Honour, can I into private session for what I want to say now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go to private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I repeat what I was saying? The running order of these witnesses we don't expect, because, of course, as Your Honours know and we know, we have expected to call witnesses in a certain order and it hasn't worked. But we've given a rough running order. We've said we're going by municipality and this is the order within the municipality, and we can produce all the various documents that we gave to Mr. Ackerman. I'm asking for -- we've had now what is anticipated to be the witnesses for the first three weeks. I'd like a running order for -- for the whole lot or at least until Christmas, again so that we can prioritise our searches. We have a unit that does this for us, but they have competing demands for other teams, and to make the best use of that unit, we need to be able to give them a running order. So, Your Honour, that's what I'm asking. Perhaps I can finish what I want to say with the -- the last on this list, so series of witnesses. And that is Your Honour will see that it is apparently intended to call witnesses from Bosanska Gradiska --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Bosanska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- Bosanska Dubica, and unless they're gone from the latest list, Glamoc appeared somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And Laktasi --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Laktasi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I have identified these -- again, not with reference to the latest of these lists, because it only arrived at 1.30, and I had prepared this already. So -- but there is Laktasi and Glamoc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we're talking of two witnesses in Laktasi and one witness in --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have two from Bosanska Gradiska and one from Bosanska Dubica. It may well be that they are considered to be important, relevant, even though Bosanska Gradiska and Bosanska Dubica are no longer in the indictment itself. But if you read the summary, this -- the summary of the intended testimony, it's -- they are going to supposedly testify on the events -- for example, let's take Gradiska, under 35. We will not say who he is or what he did. He will testify about the situation in the town before and during the war, the functioning of local authorities, the relation between them, and the ARK. This may be relevant obviously, you know, but -- but I don't know. It's -- it's something that Mr. Ackerman has to think about and decide. And if he insists on bringing forward this evidence, I -- this testimony -- witness, I can't stop him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, the reason I'm raising it, for two reasons: One, the -- Mr. Brdjanin stands in no danger of conviction in relation to any of these municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's the first thing. The second is this: What it will do, Your Honour, is open up a can of worms in the sense that in order to cut things down -- we never looked at Glamoc or Laktasi, but we -- we deliberately reduced the evidence we would call by omitting any evidence from Gradiska and Dubica. Your Honour, if any evidence is called on behalf of the Defence, then almost assuredly our application will be to call evidence in rebuttal depending, obviously, on what the evidence says, but so that Your Honours get a clearer picture, it may be, of what happened in these particular municipalities. As to Laktasi and Glamoc, which have never figured at all in this case, again, if Mr. Ackerman convinces Your Honours this is relevant and admissible to an issue in the case, then of course Your Honours no doubt will rule, but again, it will lead to the problem that our application almost certainly will be to call evidence in rebuttal relating to two municipalities about which Your Honours have heard absolutely nothing at all in the course of 18 months. So Your Honour, that's the only reason I'm raising that last part. Your Honour, and I think that's -- those are the four -- really the four aspects, that is, the -- the dates of birth, the adequacy of the summaries, the running order, and those particular municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. Let's start with the -- let's start with the last of these four, Mr. Ackerman. I will definitely not engage in any discussion with you as to whether you should or should not call these witnesses. I just want to know whether you, after having heard what Mr. -- Ms. Korner said and what I just mentioned, because I understand that -- I wouldn't even want to start thinking that you put these witnesses down not realising that Laktasi and Glamoc were not in the case. You obviously know that they are not in the case, just as much as you know that Bosanska Gradiska is no longer in the case and Bosanska Dubica is no longer in the case. So you definitely have a reason for indicating these persons in the first place. So I would like to know from you whether you are going to insist on these persons, yes or no; in which case you have to go-ahead, straight away as from now, because on a prima facie basis, even looking at the scanty summary that I have here, I don't think I can stop you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I view my obligation at this point with regard to a witness list as an obligation to furnish to the Chamber and to the Office of the Prosecutor a list of -- of all the witnesses that I know at this point that I might conceivably call as witnesses in the defence. Whether I in fact wind up calling all the people on this list is completely another matter, and I can -- and just as the Prosecutor did, I'm quite certain that this list will get whittled as we go along depending on what happens actually here in the Chamber. So I can say this: I have no intention of calling everybody that's on this list. We will not call all the people on this list, but I don't know exactly who we're going to remove at this point. With regard to those municipalities that are not within the indictment, Laktasi, Glamoc, Bosanska Dubica, those places, I certainly will not call any witnesses regarding to what one might call crime based evidence regarding that happened in those municipalities, and to some extent, these summaries were not properly written in there in the first place. There may be relevance with regard to these witnesses, Your Honour, with regard to the impact that decisions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I grant you that. I grant you that. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that's what's going on with those. With regard to witness order, Your Honour, we are actively trying to get that together. And we supplied the Prosecutor with documents and Your Honours today with documents with the witness order for the first three weeks. We have all been sitting since we got back yesterday working on this and writing larger and longer and more detailed summaries with regard to these witnesses. Now, a number of the witnesses that we're calling, Your Honour, the Prosecution has spent more time speaking with them than we have, and so if -- as Ms. Korner said, she already has the statements that they gave to us plus everything that -- that they said to them. So it's not -- we're not going to be able to enlighten her very much about some of them that she doesn't already know. I understand she's mostly concerned about those she knows virtually nothing about at this point. And we're moving through that material as rapidly as we can. And what we're trying to do is give her expanded summaries and information regarding the witnesses that we're going to be calling first. I don't want to create difficulties for the Prosecution by -- by suggesting to them some witness who we're actually going to call last is going to be called in the fourth week and make them spend a bunch of time spinning wheels about that. So I'm trying to get the order worked out. I think within a fairly reasonable time we'll be able to give a witness order through -- through the Christmas break. I don't think it will take us long to get to that point. The summaries we're just writing as fast was we can write them because we've just recently had an opportunity to speak with these witnesses at some length and ask the kind of questions that only lawyers who are familiar with the case can -- can come up with, rather than investigators who have no idea what's going on here, can't read the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We appreciate that, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that's what I'm doing with summaries. Now, I really kind of resent the allegation that I have the dates of birth of these witnesses and I'm just refusing to turn them over. I don't have them and my investigators don't have them. And I wish you could be sitting in the room when I was yelling at the investigators and telling them to please get them. And I can tell you one thing that's happened with about two or three of these witnesses: We're having a very difficult time with some witnesses, Your Honour, because they're frightened. We have witnesses who are afraid that if they come here they'll be arrested and not allowed to go home. And we explain safe conduct, we do all that sort of thing. And three of the witnesses that I know of who were called last week for their date of births refused to give them because they thought it would give the Prosecution some reason to -- to arrest them or harass them or something like that. We're making it clear to them that we can't use them if they won't give us that material rather quickly. We're trying to get it. I -- I think that's probably the highest priority that our investigators have right now is to get those. We've supplied a lot of them. We've managed to get a lot of them since the first list. If you compare the first list to this one, you'll find a lot more birth dates on it than were on the original one, and we're -- we're getting them together as quickly as we can. We certainly have them for the first -- first several witnesses that are going to be called, because the -- the VWS also requires that information, so to get there, we have to get them. And unlike the Prosecution, we don't have a unit that does this kind of thing for us, which Ms. Korner just told you about their unit that does this sort of thing for them. Again, that -- that highlights the lack of equality of arms. We don't have a unit that does anything for us. It's just the few of us who -- who labour mightily to try to -- to get where we get with this. And it would be nice if we had a unit that would do this for us and a unit that would do that for us, but only the Prosecution gets those kind of resources; we don't. I think I've covered all the things that she mentioned, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I knew -- I knew the moment -- or rather, somebody else reminded -- the moment I mentioned a unit, that Mr. Ackerman would seize upon this. Your Honour, I think I ought to make it clear, because Mr. Ackerman does say this a lot and so do other Defence counsel. The Office of the Prosecutor - and I know Your Honours know this - is dealing with hundreds and hundreds of investigations and -- and the like. It is not that everyone who's appeared in this case is individually devoted to this case. Everybody is doing other tasks at the same time. And so this -- the so-called over-mighty resources we have is because we're dealing with a large number of investigations and cases. So can I make that clear. All I want to come back on, please, is two matters. The first is Mr. Ackerman says for many of the witnesses the Prosecution know more about them than we do and, for example, those statements that we obtained. They were the only two statements that were made to the Defence that were given to us that I recall. But in any event, that's not quite the point. Even though we may have interviewed them, we may have interviewed them over a large-ranging matter -- subjects. We need to know what they're coming here to tell Your Honours about. And in fact, Your Honours need to know what they're coming to tell Your Honours about. And so we'd still like to know exactly what it is that the witnesses, even those that we've interviewed, are going to say. In respect of Glamoc and Laktasi and Gradiska and Dubica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Novi Sad as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman says he may not call them. That's all well and good, but, Your Honour, because -- particularly with the last two, they've never even formed part of our case, we're going to have to do some investigations into it and devote manpower and money to that if Mr. Ackerman is going to call evidence about it. And so, therefore, I'll ask again that it should be sooner rather than later that Mr. Ackerman tells Your Honours and us whether or not these witnesses are going to be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's fair --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that's not an unreasonable request, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's not an unreasonable request, Ms. Korner, but I don't think we can solve -- solve the matter today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, no. Your Honour, I'm sorry; I'm not saying it needs to be resolved today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know what you're --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But it does need to be resolved within, Your Honours, I would say the next month.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has a list of, I think, 291 witnesses. Never at any point did the Prosecution tell us, "You know, you can stop worrying about this witness; we're not going to call them. That never happened. They just told us the ones they were going to call from that list. They never said we've decided not to call these witnesses, although they decided that, you know, long before we ever knew they weren't coming. So I don't have any sympathy for them having to investigate witnesses that we might wind up not calling. It's what we spent hours doing for witnesses that they didn't call and probably for a long time had no intention of calling. They never gave us that information, so I don't know why we should give it to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry; I'm obviously not making myself very clear. It's not witnesses in respect of Laktasi and Glamoc. We would have to investigate the two municipalities because Your Honours could be maybe even inadvertently misled by a witness coming along from a municipality about which you've heard absolutely nothing and we've heard absolutely nothing giving you an account of things which bear very little relationship to what actually happened. And that's -- that's why I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, at the moment I am relying on my experience and -- and try to keep my mouth as shut as possible. But in reality, you ought to remember, both of you, that at the end of the day, when the moment arrives that the witness takes the witness box and starts giving evidence, if he starts saying blah, blah, blah, on things that are not relevant in our opinion, we'll stop him. So I -- I can tell you as from now that unless I am seriously convinced of the contrary, I am not interested in hearing of the events in -- in -- say, if we take Laktasi, he can testify about the events in Laktasi before and during the war. Are we interested in those? I mean, I concede to Mr. Ackerman that he has conceded already that maybe the summaries here have not been crafted in -- in as desirable a fashion as possible. But apart from that, if he -- if he takes the witness box -- the witness stand to testify on Brdjanin's role because Brdjanin also had a role in -- in the events of the municipality of Laktasi, we'll see -- we'll see what the relevance is and we'll take it up from there. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt you, particularly the interpreters, but Your Honour, it's a bit late then when the witness is in the witness box when we don't know what he's going to say. Unless Your Honours make a ruling here and now -- well, not here and now but within a short period of time, that if any witness from this municipality is to be called, the only aspect on which he will be allowed to testify is any relationship between himself and Mr. Brdjanin. But if, Your Honour, it goes further than that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or also Brdjanin's -- Brdjanin's role. Also Brdjanin's role. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. But then I have to know that. And I think the best thing is that Your Honour at least orders that summaries for these potential witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, the actual problem is the summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- that we get full and proper summaries of what it is anticipated these witnesses from Laktasi and Glamoc will say, and that to be done before almost anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, what have I said today to cause the Prosecution to believe we're not going to give them summaries? I've said over and over that we're working on the summaries. And it doesn't make any difference who the witness is, they're going to get summaries of exactly what they're coming here to talk about. I mean, this is just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to improve in that -- in that sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at the materials I gave you today, Your Honour, they contain much more detailed summaries than are in the witness lists. And that's what we're doing, we're writing those summaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, that I realise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's what we're doing. Some of the witnesses we have statements from and those will be turned over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But let's -- let's -- because what you're saying makes sense and what Ms. Korner raised earlier on also is justified. Laktasi, Glamoc, Novi Grad, and -- and Bosanska Dubica, Bosanska Gradiska to a lesser extent. I can't -- I can't expect from the Prosecution to be prepared to deal with any of the witnesses that you bring forward coming from these municipalities if I know that the -- the Prosecution has not had any need at all to conduct any investigations or -- or obtain more information on what happened in these municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I make it clear. I can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please, please, please, let me try to stop this. Because let me just make it really clear: We are not, as I said before, opening any crime-based issues with regard to any of these municipalities. The only reason that we might call those witnesses have to do with the relationship of that municipality to the ARK Crisis Staff or the relationship of Mr. Brdjanin to that municipality, and that's the information you need to know and I just gave it to you. I'll give it to you in more detail at a later time, but I am not going to open that whole can of worms that she talks about. I've said it twice now; that should be enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough, Mr. Ackerman. And I would agree with you, if you restrict it to this, because it makes sense. But the Prosecution ought to know because what you say in the summary is not that. If you refer to number 57, without saying who he was or what position he occupied, just -- he can testify about the events before, during the war, and his relation with Mr. Brdjanin. Let's reserve the last part and say that is relevant even -- on the face of it even though it is as scanty as can be. But what does the rest have to -- have got to do with the matters that we are discussing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely nothing. It shouldn't have been in there in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Granted. So let's move along the direction that I mentioned before. I conceded that -- you conceded that the crafting of this other is unfortunate, as it is here. It's -- well, I read this. I -- obviously I have the same feeling that you have. You should be in a -- put in a position. But if it's going to be restricted to -- I was going to give an example myself, but Mr. Ackerman himself brought the matter up. If it's a question of, for example, the relationship or -- between that particular municipality and Mr. Brdjanin or the ARK Crisis Staff, obviously there is relevance -- relevance there. But you ought to know. This is -- this is where I definitely agree 100 per cent with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, in fact, it's -- I see although it's listed under Laktasi, number 57 is in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, I know --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- but I don't want to -- I don't want to mention the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Then this is Srbac apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But I don't know where Srbac is. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just saying this: First of all, Novi Grad is actually Bosanski Novi. It's the Serb name for it. So we do know -- Your Honours have heard evidence about Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But secondly, it's -- it's not, in our view, going to be possible to divorce what happened in a municipality from someone testifying about the relationship of the Crisis Staff in that municipality and Mr. Brdjanin, because one of the -- the major planks, of course, in this case is that regardless of the technical legality or illegality of the Regional Crisis Staff, the Municipal Crisis Staff implemented the decisions. And to show the implementation of those decisions, you would have to look at what actually happened. And that's the difficulty. So Your Honour, I've raised the issue, and I think all we can do now is wait for your -- for Mr. Ackerman to provide a proper summary of what these witness will be saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, Ms. Korner. I think so. I think the message has been well taken by -- by us and by Mr. Ackerman, and I'm sure Mr. Ackerman will help us in the right direction. So anything else, Ms. Korner, before I continue myself?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, I think that's all we wanted to raise about the -- about the Defence witness list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's take the rest bit by bit. The revised list of witnesses, however complete or incomplete it may be, is, as I take it, Mr. Ackerman, still subject to modifications as we go along?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- the modifications would be, you know, if -- if we somehow encounter a -- a highly relevant witness that we believe needs to be called to complete the picture in this case, we -- we would certainly ask leave to add that person. But the major modification of this list as we go along is going to be reduction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Reduction. Okay. You also stated somewhere that at present there are no witnesses which you intend to bring forward to testify pursuant to Rule 92 bis. Is that still the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's still the position. There is one now that we are considering that with regard to, but we probably won't do it. The problem is, Your Honour, we -- we're not doing crime base witnesses, so virtually any witness we call has to do with acts and conducts of the accused, and that would not be a 92 bis possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I would have imagined that that part was intended to be to the advantage of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I -- I would think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's -- in other words, the right to object.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, maybe. It's my view that Ms. Korner would object if the witness is going to go into the acts and conducts of the accused and would want to cross-examine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She has a right to object obviously, but I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I don't think you ought to put in the same basket, at the same level, the Prosecution and the Defence when it comes to reading that article, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the Rule -- is Rule certainly doesn't make a distinction, Your Honour. It applies to both sides equally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I grant you that but --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I put it this way -- sorry. If Mr. Ackerman has a statement that says Mr. Brdjanin is kind dogs and cats, I hardly think that I'm going to ask for the witness to be called to be cross-examined. It's a question of fact and degree in each case. Your Honour, I'm so sorry, there was one other matter. I'm sorry to interrupt Your Honour again, but I forgot about that. It goes back to the ruling that Your Honour made a very long time ago in January 2002 about the defendant testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm coming to that. Don't worry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honour was going to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm coming to that. In fact, it's the very last thing I -- and I'm also prepared to refer to the case law of this Tribunal on the matter. So, Mr. Ackerman, we can cut this short. You have also indicated and you have repeated it several times today, that you -- there is a possibility of reducing this list. You actually stated elsewhere that there is also a possibility -- that you may be able to reduce your case by a third. Do you have an indication already as to which third that would be? I mean, if you refer to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or is it still very vague in your mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's extraordinarily difficult at this point to project how long -- because I've not seen the Prosecution do any cross-examination yet. It's impossible to predict in my mind right now how long these witnesses are going to take when you add on the cross-examination how many of these witnesses we will be able to put on very rapidly. And I don't think we will call one witness that took as long as some of the Prosecution witnesses. So we'll -- we'll move through witnesses a lot more rapidly, I think, than the Prosecution did in some respect. But I don't know how long the cross-examinations will take, of course. The other thing: Our current planning right now is that the expert witnesses would be called near the very end of the case, and we expect that will be in January. And so we're believing that -- that we can finish before the end of January. That's -- that's our hope, which should be, I think, three or four weeks ahead of -- of the amount of time we've been given, because I think -- I think, if I look at the schedule properly, we're -- we're scheduled through the end of February. I think we can be finished before that. We'll certainly -- we certainly -- I can't imagine that we would go -- even try to go beyond the number of weeks that you've allotted for the matter. And that would include - and I'll tell you now, although I failed to bring the date today - we have -- we have not completed, and I eluded to it earlier -- we have not completed the work that we absolutely must do in Bosnia. And I'll be applying to you for about a seven-day adjournment, I think in November, so that we can return to Bosnia and complete our work there. That does not change my view as to when we will complete the case. But we really do need to go back there and finish the work that we've -- that we've started there, because what I -- what I will not do, Your Honour, is -- is bring witnesses here at the expense of the Tribunal, sit and talk with them, and decide to send them home because I'm not going to use them. So I insist on speaking to the witnesses personally before I will bring them here and put the Tribunal to the expense of bringing them here. I need to speak to a few more people there, and we'll be finished with that process. The end is -- is in sight, but we think we need about a seven-day adjournment to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that, Mr. Ackerman. If you could let us have well in advance the dates when you would like this break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it's the 13th of November, Your Honour. What I'm asking for is the Friday of -- of -- I can probably tell you right now. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because we have got, all of us, other work to do and we can use that time frame for other cases that we are handling with. If we -- if we get the Maglov contempt case on that particular week, do you require to be here, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. All right. So which week did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It looks -- I'm now a little bit confused, Your Honour, but I think -- I think the week we have in mind is that we would off on the 15th of November and resume on the 26th. So we -- we would not sit on the 15th and we would not sit on the 25th. And then the week -- that intervening week. I believe that's what we have in mind as to what would work well for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The 25th is what day? The 26th is what day?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The 25th is a Monday, and the -- and that's also -- and then the -- the 15th is a Friday. So we would not sit on that Friday, then we would have the full week off, not sit on the following Monday, and resume on the 26th, which is a Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well -- I'm wrong about that. That's all wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you can confirm this to us as early as you can, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's actually the 14th is the Friday and the 24th is the Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you can let us have --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- the fixed dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll put it in writing and send it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. Thank you. So -- I take it also, Mr. Ackerman, that -- I barely need to say this, but I will say it: If you intend at any one stage to go beyond the list of witnesses, in other words, to bring forward additional witnesses, then we will require good prior notice, and not just me but in particular the Prosecution. I mean, we -- we can live with a shorter time, but the Prosecution needs to know in particular. All right? So it's -- it's an understanding. That has been dealt with, Bosanska Gradiska, Dubica, Laktasi, Glamoc. There are some witnesses that you referred to even in the revised list as very tentative witnesses. Are you still there, or shall we leave them as tentative -- very tentative witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I thought I had moved -- removed that language. That was -- that was not intended to be disclosed. But if -- if Your Honour has one that says "very tentative," it's true. They are very tentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I didn't mean for that to get in the disclosure, because that tends to be kind of internal information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I ask of you, Mr. Ackerman, as we go along and you make up your mind, to update us from time to time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's -- that's what I intend to do. I'll be filing -- I'm going to use that same template that Your Honours have, and I'll just be filing updates to it with you. So I'll be removing witnesses from it and I'll be adding material like birth dates to it, and things of that nature. But I'd like to use that same template so you'll have a running --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll tell you why. Because the approach that we are taking is a very -- a very simple one, actually. I mean, if we stick to the time frame that you indicate, there are obviously no problems. So I don't -- I don't foresee any problems. But as you rightly said, a trial is a trial and anything can happen on any given day and a witness who is expected to testify for half a day ends up being here for two days or three days. It has happened in the past and it will definitely happen in the future. So we may well end up with a situation which is different from what we have now, which may require us to revisit the whole thing. So I'm making this very clear. Today I am definitely not -- we've discussed this -- I am not in favour of fixing a maximum number of witnesses that you can bring forward, but as we go along, if I see that your estimates were completely wrong and that there is no way we could finish this case before a certain time limit, then we will need to talk again and possibly - possibly, not necessarily - review the position. That's not to be excluded that I will fix -- that we will fix a number of days or time limit within which you need to -- to finish, just as we did with the -- with the Prosecution. We are at the moment happy with your anticipation that you can finish this by the end of January. So we are not going to -- to take any radical decisions. We don't think we need to at this point in time. But if things -- the situation changes, obviously we need to think twice about this. And remembering what we had talked about months ago when we were arguing on how and when the case of -- of the Prosecution was to finish. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, can I just ask: The estimate that Mr. Ackerman has given to Your Honours, is that to include cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. This is it. But I think he's venturing into -- I mean, I don't want to comment myself, but -- because I don't know these witnesses and I don't know what you know about these witnesses, and I can't even imagine how much time you will require to cross-examine these witnesses properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour will have seen that one of the witnesses, who's number 2 on the list, I think he is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Some of them -- yeah, I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour -- Your Honour will imagine that from what everything Your Honour has heard in this case he is likely to be there for some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But you also realise that here, for example, you have two days. Already in the summary that you were given --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's two to three, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- it's already gone up to three. I wouldn't be surprised if this person stays here with us the entire week. I wouldn't be surprised in the least. But then one thing compensates for -- for the other. If you have a number of witnesses reduced -- I think we have to play it by the ear as we go along and then decide accordingly. But I am leaving all options open; in other words, when you say 60 witnesses, 58, 64, I am not contesting that for the time being. Certainly not. I am not establishing a maximum number of witnesses. I am not establishing a deadline for the termination of your Defence, since you indicate the end of January. I'm not even -- I'm not even threatening that if I anticipate that we are going further by one week, that's going to be -- or two weeks, that's going to cause major problems. But we reserve our position as we -- as we go -- as we go along. The idea is, for the time being, that more or less you anticipate that give and take you should be able to finish your case by around the -- the end of -- the end of January?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's certainly the plan, Your Honour. My greatest fear regarding witnesses is that I will bring too few at a time rather than too many, and wind up with days that we can't do anything because we have no witnesses. And that's a very difficult call to make, and I certainly hate to -- to put the Tribunal to the expense of having people sit around here for days and days waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the same problem -- that's the same problem that the Prosecution had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Prosecution had the same problem. I think they handled it admirably, by the way. I don't know if I'll be able to do as well as they did. They seemed always to have someone available without too much inconvenience - there was some - but let's hope that we can do as well as they did in that regard. We will try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman, I notice going through your list, your revised list, that there are a number of witnesses for whom you will be seeking protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. The Trial Chamber will deal with those as they appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll be filing -- I'll be filing something, you know, as soon as I can with regard to them. I think there will be probably less than -- than is shown there. I -- I strongly -- I very strongly encourage people to testify in -- in open session. You know -- you know my proclivities about that. And so I resist pretty strongly people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It may not always be possible. You may find yourself in a situation where you yourself will be asking for closed sessions. But anyway. The same applies for safe conducts, in case these are required. But I don't think I need to say anything myself on that. And the very last note that I had put here precisely reflects what Ms. Korner had stated earlier, that I would like you -- the Trial Chamber - when say I, it's the Trial Chamber, Judge Janu and Judge Taya with me - to provide the order of witnesses that you intend to bring forward, to give it some -- some order so that the Prosecution may -- may be able to cope. And also, we tried to adopt the system that we adopted during the case of the Prosecution, so that you provide the list, then, of the witnesses for the following week or in time during the previous week. And I would -- I think we were having Thursday as the deadline for the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was Thursday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But I think we can do a great deal better than that because we -- we don't have any motive to -- to withhold information. Our motive is to supply information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I am not -- we are not placing any order. We are just basing -- relying on your cooperation on this. And if there are problems later on, then we will -- it's taken that you will start with your first witness on the 20th of October, and we come to the last point, which also has been mentioned by Ms. Korner, and that is will your client be testifying. And if so, a question of at which point he offers his testimony becomes important in the light of the case law of this Tribunal and also the case law of several jurisdictions, including the jurisdictions from where you come, Mr. Ackerman. My jurisdiction, for example: We insist that if the accused is going to give evidence, to offer his evidence, he will be the first witness obviously in his own defence. That's -- yeah, there is no way he can then offer his testimony at the end of -- of -- after that -- his other witnesses have given evidence. The same system applies or obtains in many countries. Over here it has been recognised that the option of the accused testifying at the end, after all the other witnesses have testified, cannot be ruled out. But there may be consequences. I am sure that you will be discussing this with your client. I am not insisting to have a reply today, obviously, because I don't quite know whether your client has been prepared for this and I don't quite know whether you were prepared to face this question, but it is one question that we will face you with again very soon. But I want to make sure that your client is made aware that -- first that he has a right not -- not to offer his testimony. That's number one; he has a right. No one can force him to give evidence. Secondly, if he arrives at the decision to give evidence, then he has these two options, the first of which is the safest or safer of the two. So that's the position. And perhaps when we meet again, you should be in a position to give us a feedback on this. All right? Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously if the defendant is going to testify, as opposed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- to make a statement, we had a lengthy and occasionally heated discussion in the course of the Stakic case about this. But I understand what Judge Schomburg was referring to by a statement of the accused is not testifying and doesn't carry that weight. But Your Honours' original ruling was he should, if he's going to testify, testify first. But it is absolutely clear to me and to Your Honour that the -- this is perhaps not as clear-cut in this Tribunal as in our own jurisdictions. However, all I'm asking is -- Mr. Ackerman, of course, has the right to make an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I was just wondering as a matter of administration whether he was going to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm coming to that. Because -- this is the last one. Because we all agree that we are starting on the 20th with his first witness. But if -- is he going to make an opening statement and when?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I toiled with that quite a bit over the last several weeks and concluded that I have fairly effectively done that already by the way I've cross-examined witnesses and the suggestions I've made in the process of cross-examining witnesses. So I think I'll decline to make an opening statement and just start with witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But it's good to know I mean because reading between the lines, that's what I thought the position would be. But I've been reminded that this is always a possibility and I need to put the question. So if you change your mind, Mr. Ackerman, you are to advise the -- inform the Prosecution and us, of course, but the Prosecution first and foremost. Any other matter you would like to raise, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour. I -- I would just like to kind of as a -- as a closing remark say that -- that I really appreciate the Chamber's understanding of the difficulties under which we're operating and -- and I want to assure you that in return we will just do everything we can to -- to make this matter run as smoothly as possible and as -- with as little difficulty as possible. And our motive is the same as yours, and that is to conclude this case in a just and honourable way as quickly as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. The Chamber, Mr. Ackerman, is always full of understanding and always tries to cooperate. The only problem that there is - and I need to make this clear to both of you, actually - is that we have the Rules. We are not the only Chamber here functioning. And this is not the only trial functioning. And I -- I cannot face the rest of the other Judges and the Tribunal if I fail to apply the Rules. And the Rules are, as you are all aware, the Rules are changed from time to time. Practically now there is an obsession of trying to find an extra way, an additional way in which we can reduce the length of the proceedings, reduce the length of the trial without endangering the rights of -- of the defendant, which is indeed something that we are all keen upon. But we will only react if we are put in the position where we are exposed to criticism of not applying the Rules or being too open-handed and too a largesse which is not conducive to a speedy conclusion of this trial. So you cooperate in this and you will find us very cooperative in the rest. Okay? I thank you. We will meet again, please God, on Monday. I think we are sitting in the morning, Chuqing, or in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we're sitting all mornings next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just on the timing again, Your Honour. We're not objecting to Mr. Ackerman's request for a week. Can we take it that if Mr. Ackerman puts the request in for this week, being the 16th or whatever it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 16th to 25th, he says.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That Your Honours will be granting that request?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will be waiting to hear from you first, because maybe that week is not very acceptable to you or maybe you want -- you event want to object to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm not going to object to it, to the time that Mr. Ackerman wants. If it were left to us, it would be more suitable for various operational reasons if Mr. Ackerman could make it the week of the -- the following week as opposed to the week he's picked. But if Mr. Ackerman has already made his arrangements, then it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't know the dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've not already made the arrangements, Your Honour, and I may very well accede to that request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The important thing is that you let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because we will fit in other -- other work that we have pending, both of us, the three of us, actually. So if we know well in advance, that would be extremely helpful. All right? I thank you. Have a nice evening, a nice weekend. And we will meet on Monday morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: adjourned at 6.05 p.m. The hearing will reconvene on Monday, the 13th day of October, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
